# autosquash and fixup: fold fix commits into their targets

After this page you can stage changes as targeted fixup commits using `git commit --fixup`, automatically reorder and meld those fixups during an interactive rebase with `git rebase -i --autosquash`, and understand how to clean up branch history without manual todo-list editing.

## Thesis

During code review or development, you often need to address feedback or fix typos on commits created earlier in your branch. Instead of amending previous commits interactively or making loose "fix typo" commits that clutter git history, **`git commit --fixup`** labels temporary commits with a special prefix (`fixup! <commit-message>` or `squash! <commit-message>`). 

When combined with **`git rebase -i --autosquash`**, Git automatically pairs each fixup commit with its original target commit in the interactive todo list, reordering them so the fixup line sits directly below its target set to `fixup` action. When the rebase runs, Git melds the fix into the target commit and discards the extra commit message, producing a clean, logical history.

Verified below with **git 2.47.3**.

## Mental model

```text
 working tree changes                 commit history               rebase --autosquash todo

                                     0ec36b4 feature B
                                            │                        pick 6ef5195 feature A
                                            ▼                        fixup 191b874 fixup! feature A
  edit files for feature A     ──►   191b874 fixup! feature A ──►    pick 0ec36b4 feature B
                                            │                          │
                                            ▼                          ▼
                                     6ef5195 feature A             melded into single
                                                                   commit: f76fe12 feature A
```

Instead of manually running `git rebase -i`, searching for the SHA of `feature A`, moving the fixup line up, and changing `pick` to `fixup`, Git performs the reordering and action assignment automatically.

## Mechanics: commit options and configuration

| Command / Setting | Purpose |
|-------------------|---------|
| `git commit --fixup=<commit>` | Creates a commit with subject `fixup! <target-commit-subject>`. |
| `git commit --squash=<commit>` | Creates a commit with subject `squash! <target-commit-subject>` (preserves commit message for editing during rebase). |
| `git rebase -i --autosquash <upstream>` | Triggers interactive rebase and automatically reorders fixup/squash commits under their targets. |
| `rebase.autoSquash` | Config knob (`git config rebase.autoSquash true`) to enable `--autosquash` automatically for all interactive rebases. |

## Interactive todo list generation

When you invoke `git rebase -i --autosquash`, Git scans the commit range for commit messages starting with `fixup!` or `squash!`. It matches the subject text following the prefix against earlier commits in the commit range.

If a match is found, Git moves the fixup commit line immediately below the target commit line and changes its command from `pick` to `fixup` (or `squash`).

Running an interactive rebase across a branch demonstrates how Git prepares the todo list.

To generate the todo list automatically for a commit range:
```bash
git rebase -i --autosquash a079db8
```

=== autosquash todo ===
pick 6ef5195 feature A
fixup 191b874 fixup! feature A
pick 0ec36b4 feature B

# Rebase a079db8..191b874 onto a079db8 (3 commands)
#
# Commands:
# p, pick <commit> = use commit
# r, reword <commit> = use commit, but edit the commit message
# e, edit <commit> = use commit, but stop for amending
# s, squash <commit> = use commit, but meld into previous commit
# f, fixup [-C | -c] <commit> = like "squash" but keep only the previous
#                    commit's log message, unless -C is used, in which case
#                    keep only this commit's message; -c is same as -C but
#                    opens the editor
# x, exec <command> = run command (the rest of the line) using shell
# b, break = stop here (continue rebase later with 'git rebase --continue')
# d, drop <commit> = remove commit
# l, label <label> = label current HEAD with a name
# t, reset <label> = reset HEAD to a label
# m, merge [-C <commit> | -c <commit>] <label> [# <oneline>]
#         create a merge commit using the original merge commit's
#         message (or the oneline, if no original merge commit was
#         specified); use -c <commit> to reword the commit message
# u, update-ref <ref> = track a placeholder for the <ref> to be updated
#                       to this position in the new commits. The <ref> is
#                       updated at the end of the rebase
#
# These lines can be re-ordered; they are executed from top to bottom.
#
# If you remove a line here THAT COMMIT WILL BE LOST.
#
# However, if you remove everything, the rebase will be aborted.
#
=== log after ===
d80ab67 feature B
f76fe12 feature A
a079db8 root
=== f.txt in feature A (HEAD~1) ===
fix

Notice how commit `191b874` (`fixup! feature A`) was originally created after `0ec36b4` (`feature B`), but the autosquash engine reordered it directly below `6ef5195` (`feature A`) and set the operation to `fixup`.

After saving and closing the interactive rebase editor, Git applies the reordered todo list and combines the history.

To inspect the commit history after completing the rebase:
```bash
git log --oneline
```

=== autosquash todo ===

fixup 191b874 fixup! feature A

To verify that the changes from the fixup commit were successfully folded into the original feature commit:
```bash
git show HEAD~1:f.txt
```

## Lab: complete autosquash workflow

<!-- file: autosquash-lab.sh -->
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Recreate autosquash and fixup demonstration (git 2.47.x).
set -euo pipefail
rm -rf /tmp/autosquash-demo && mkdir /tmp/autosquash-demo && cd /tmp/autosquash-demo
git init -b main
git config user.name "Author Name"
git config user.email "author@example.com"

# Create initial root commit
echo "base" > root.txt
git add root.txt
git commit -m "root"

# Create feature A
echo "initial feature A" > f.txt
git add f.txt
git commit -m "feature A"

# Create feature B
echo "feature B" > b.txt
git add b.txt
git commit -m "feature B"

# Address feedback on feature A using --fixup
echo "fix" > f.txt
git add f.txt
git commit --fixup=HEAD~1

# Run non-interactive autosquash rebase using GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true
GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true git rebase -i --autosquash HEAD~3

echo "=== log after ==="
git log --oneline

echo "=== f.txt in feature A (HEAD~1) ==="
git show HEAD~1:f.txt
```

## Advanced usage: amend and reword fixups

Git extends the `--fixup` flag to support targeted rewording or amending without manually stopping at a commit during rebase:

```bash
git commit --fixup=amend:<commit>   # Creates an amend! commit that replaces content and message
git commit --fixup=reword:<commit>  # Creates a reword! commit that edits subject/body only
```

When `--autosquash` runs against `amend:` or `reword:` commits:
- `amend:<commit>` converts to `fixup -C <commit>` in the todo list, keeping the fixup commit's message while discarding the original.
- `reword:<commit>` converts to `fixup -c <commit>` in the todo list, opening an editor to modify the commit message.

## Common mistakes

1. **Targeting by commit subject after modifying subject.** If you target `--fixup=<commit>` using subject matching and later reword the target commit before running `--autosquash`, Git will not find a match and leaves the fixup commit at its original position as `pick`.
2. **Forgetting `--autosquash` flag (or `rebase.autoSquash` config).** Running `git rebase -i` without `--autosquash` leaves fixup commits as `pick` in their original chronological order, requiring manual reordering.
3. **Fixup commits pushed to shared remote branches.** Fixup commits are meant for local cleanup. Pushing raw `fixup!` commits to a shared upstream branch forces teammates to review fragmented history. Always run `git rebase -i --autosquash` before requesting final integration.
4. **Targeting commits outside the rebase range.** If the target commit is older than the `<upstream>` revision supplied to `git rebase -i --autosquash`, Git cannot move the fixup commit behind the upstream point and warns that the target commit was not found.

## Best practices

- Enable global autosquashing via `git config --global rebase.autoSquash true` so every interactive rebase automatically reorganizes fixups.
- Combine with `git commit --fixup=HEAD` or `git commit --fixup=@~2` using commit references during active development to avoid looking up SHAs.
- Use `git log --oneline` prior to squashing to ensure all `fixup!` commits match valid targets on your topic branch.

## Summary

- `git commit --fixup=<commit>` creates a lightweight commit tagged specifically to fold into a target commit.
- `git rebase -i --autosquash` automatically matches `fixup!` and `squash!` commits, reorders them below targets, and assigns the appropriate action.
- Enable `rebase.autoSquash=true` in your Git configuration to avoid passing the flag manually.
- Use fixups locally during peer code review to maintain clean, bisectable commit histories without manual todo-list editing.
